mcqs.question: `const params = new URLSearchParams('?tag=react&tag=vue&tag=react')`. What do `params.getAll('tag')` and `params.get('tag')` return?
options: `['react']` and `'react'` — `getAll` collapses repeated keys and `get` returns the only value
`['react', 'vue', 'react']` and `'react'` — every value in document order, and `get` returns the first
`['react', 'vue', 'react']` and `'react,vue,react'` — `get` joins the repeated values into a string
`['react', 'vue', 'react']` and `'vue'` — a repeated key lets the last value win
mcqs.explanation: `getAll` keeps every value for the key, in the order they appear, duplicates included, and returns strings: `['react', 'vue', 'react']`. `get` returns the first match, `'react'`, and `null` when the key is absent. The strongest distractor is the last-wins option: it borrows the semantics of object parsing and of `set()`, which *replaces* every existing value for a key, while `append()` adds one more (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams). Writing replaces, reading reports — that asymmetry is the whole trap, and a first `set()` followed by `append()` calls is exactly where the confusion is born. The 'collapses' and 'joins' options are the same mistake in the other direction, assuming the browser normalizes a repeated key into one value when deduping and joining are steps the caller has to write (`new Set(...)`, `join(',')`). Because nothing is deduplicated or sorted for you, a multi-value filter has to be deduped and ordered explicitly before it becomes a cache key.

mcqs.question: `Total` runs `const totalAtom = atom((get) => get(priceAtom) * factor)` on every render and subscribes with `useAtomValue(totalAtom)`; an effect then calls `onTotalChange(total)`, which updates parent state. Typing in a sibling input makes that effect fire again. What does Jotai do with the recreated definition?
options: Atoms are cached by their read function, so the recreated definition reuses the first atom and only the value recomputes
Each render creates a new atom — a new store node with its own subscription and no shared value with the previous one — so the component resubscribes and the effect runs again
Each render creates a new atom, but Jotai carries the previous value over because the read function reads the same `priceAtom`
Nothing is wrong with the definition itself; the effect loops because `factor` is closed over instead of being read from its own atom
mcqs.explanation: An atom config is a plain object, so its identity is the reference: a definition created during render is a different atom on every render — another node in the store, another subscription, and no shared value with the previous one, which is why the effect sees a 'new' value and feeds the loop back into the parent. Dependency tracking is not affected, because dependencies are discovered at read time through `get` (https://jotai.org/docs/core/atom); what changes is which atom the component is subscribed to. The strongest distractor is the carry-over option: it reasons from values ('same reads, same result, so surely Jotai reuses it'), but atoms are keyed by identity, so there is no previous atom to reuse. The function-caching option is the same category error with a memoization story attached. The closure option points at a real smell but leaves `atom(...)` in the render body, so identity still churns; the stable versions are `useMemo(() => atom(...), [factor])`, hoisting the definition when it has no props, or `atomFamily(factor)` when one atom per key is genuinely needed.

mcqs.question: `InvoicesTable` renders `invoices` from the query cache, supports filtering and sorting, and opens a drawer for the clicked row. Each refetch returns fresh `Invoice` objects, and changing the sort reorders the list. What should the drawer keep as its state?
options: The clicked `Invoice` object, because it already holds every field the drawer renders
The clicked row's index, because a number is cheap and cannot go stale
The clicked `invoice.id`, resolved against the current array when the drawer renders
The clicked `Invoice` object, plus an effect that copies the matching item out of the array whenever the array changes
mcqs.explanation: An id is the only value that names the selection while the data keeps moving: it survives a refetch that returns new objects with the same ids and a re-sort that moves the row, and the drawer renders whatever the cache holds now, so it cannot show a stale snapshot. That is the derivation direction the state-structure guidance recommends — store the minimum, derive the rest (https://react.dev/learn/choosing-the-state-structure). The strongest distractor is the stored object: it looks like the honest thing to keep, but a refetch replaces the array elements, so the drawer keeps rendering the object it captured while the table renders the new one — the duplicated state behind 'avoid duplication in state'. The index option fails on any reorder or filter: index 3 points at a different invoice after sorting by amount, and may not exist after filtering. The object-plus-effect version is that same duplication wearing reconciliation machinery, and it still needs a policy for the selected row disappearing; the plain id gets that for free — resolve it, and if it is gone, close the drawer or say the row left the current filter.

mcqs.question: A route-level 'new post' composer writes `draftTitle`, `draftBody`, `isDirty` and `isSaving` to the Redux store on every keystroke. Nothing outside the composer reads them, and every visit has to dispatch `resetDraft()` because the store kept the text from the previous one. Following the form-state boundary in the bank, where should that state live?
options: Keep the slice and also reset from the composer's unmount cleanup, so the next visit starts empty
In the composer's own state; the server cache holds the persisted post and is invalidated after a successful submit
In the query cache under a dedicated `draft` key, so it survives navigation and is deduplicated like other server data
In both the store and the query cache, with the submit handler deciding which copy wins
mcqs.explanation: The draft is short-lived, single-reader, workflow-scoped state: the form creates it, the form dies with it, nothing else needs it — the definition of the form boundary. After submit the persisted post is server state, so it belongs to the query cache and gets invalidated. The strongest distractor is the unmount cleanup: it looks like a one-line fix and keeps a session-lifetime owner for a screen-lifetime value, so the reset only exists *because* the store outlives the screen; the slice stays writable from anywhere, and any exit that skips the cleanup (a full reload, the back button into a restored tree, a route guard redirect) brings the old text back. The query-cache option confuses a cache with an input buffer: a draft has no server lifecycle, nothing to invalidate and no staleness to reason about, and one write per keystroke gives one cache entry per character. The fourth option is the second writable copy the bank warns about, with a manual winner-picking step that is exactly the reconciliation the boundary avoids. The stated exception still holds: if the draft must outlive the screen — a multi-step wizard across routes — then a dedicated slice or the URL is justified.

mcqs.question: A search box must show only the latest query's results. Which operator makes that the default behavior?
options: switchMap: it cancels the previous inner request when a new one starts
concatMap: it queues queries and runs them in order
exhaustMap: it ignores new queries while one is in flight
mergeMap: it runs every query concurrently
mcqs.explanation: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner observable, so only the latest query can update the UI. concatMap preserves order but lets stale results arrive late; exhaustMap drops queries; mergeMap interleaves them.

mcqs.question: What does a memoized selector give you in NgRx?
options: Derived views recomputed only when their input slice of state changes
Mutable state that components can write to directly
Automatic HTTP caching for effects
Time-travel debugging by itself
mcqs.explanation: Selectors derive read views from the store and memoize on their inputs, so components recompute only when the state they depend on changes. The store stays immutable and owned by reducers.

mcqs.question: A preferences object is read by three components on different routes, changes only when the user edits settings, and has no complex update coordination. Following the state-scope decision in the bank, who should own it?
options: A global store, because more than one component reads the value
Local state in each of the three components, kept in sync with an effect
Context from the closest common provider: readers are distant, but updates are simple and infrequent
A global store when the data comes from the server, and Context otherwise
mcqs.explanation: Distance decides whether sharing is needed, not how much machinery to add. Context already removes prop drilling for a subtree, and with simple, infrequent updates there is no coordination or inspection payoff that would justify a store (https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context). The strongest distractor is 'a global store because more than one component reads it': it equates shared with global, but two readers are handled by one provider, while a store earns its place when updates are frequent or complex, many writers must agree, or state must be inspected consistently over time (https://redux.js.org/faq/general). The last option confuses ownership with placement: server-owned data belongs in the server-state cache whichever container the client state uses.

mcqs.question: An `AuthProvider` renders `<AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, login }}>` where `login` is recreated on every render and `user` is unchanged. Its parent re-renders for an unrelated reason. What happens below the provider?
options: Nothing re-renders, because `user` is the same object and React compares context values field by field
Only the direct children re-render; deeper consumers are shielded once they are wrapped in `memo`
Consumers re-render only if they also receive changed props alongside the context read
Every component that reads `AuthContext` below the provider re-renders, including ones wrapped in `memo`
mcqs.explanation: Context compares the whole `value` by `Object.is`, and an inline object literal has a new identity on every provider render, so consumers receive a new value even though `user` is unchanged. A context subscription lives on the consumer, and `memo` cannot block it because the update does not arrive as a prop (https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext). The strongest distractor is the field-by-field comparison: it sounds like React does structural equality, but a single reference comparison is exactly why the inline object is the classic accidental trigger; `useMemo` over `[user, login]` plus `useCallback` for `login` is the fix. The neighbouring distractor is the related but wrong belief that `memo` protects consumers, when it only protects the props path.

mcqs.question: A theme toggle must survive reloads and the page is server-rendered. Which sequence keeps hydration correct?
options: `useState(() => localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light')` so the first client render already shows the saved theme
Render a fixed default first, read `localStorage` in an effect after mount, then update; if the value must be right on first paint, serialize it into the server output
Branch on `typeof window` during render: the server returns the default and the client reads storage
Read the theme from a module-level variable during render so the server and the client share the same value
mcqs.explanation: Hydration attaches React to server HTML and requires the first client render to produce the same output the server produced. `localStorage` is browser-only, so a fixed default is rendered first, the effect reads storage after hydration, and the update lands in a normal re-render; when the persisted value cannot wait, the server must serialize the same snapshot so both sides agree from the start (https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot). The strongest distractor is the lazy initializer: it is the idiomatic read-once pattern in a client-only app and even saves one render, but during hydration it makes the client's first render differ from the server markup, which is precisely the mismatch this question is about. The `typeof window` branch creates two different trees, and a module-level variable is per-process state that does not exist as a shared snapshot between server and client.

scenarios.prompt: Symptom: a user opens profile settings, types a new display name, pauses, and the input snaps back to the stored name. On a slow connection the revert also lands right after clicking Save, and the request goes out with the pre-edit value. Returning to the tab (focus refetch) makes it happen more often. Explain the mechanism, then state the state and reconciliation policy you would implement, including what happens when the user opens a different record.

code.caption: The display name snaps back mid-edit, and Save can send the value from before the edit.

rubric: Names the mechanism: each refetch returns a new `Profile` object, so the `[profile]` effect reseeds the draft and wipes the edited field; the timing follows focus/reconnect, not user actions.
Seeds once per record identity (key/remount or an explicit reset on id change) instead of seeding from data-keyed effects, and notices the draft is seeded twice here.
Tracks dirty per field and merges server values into untouched fields only.
Handles the field that is both dirty and changed remotely explicitly — conflict UI or a 409 with a version/ETag — instead of last-write-wins.
Resets the baseline from the mutation response and distinguishes a record change from a background refresh.

scenarios.prompt: The app mounts once, then the user clicks the theme button inside `Sidebar`. Predict exactly which `render …` lines appear on the first mount and again after that single click, explain why `memo` does not save `UserBadge`, and refactor the providers so a theme change no longer re-renders session consumers.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Prediction. On the first mount every component mounts once: `render AppProviders`, `render Sidebar`, `render UserBadge`, `render Footer`. After the single click the log shows `render AppProviders`, `render Sidebar`, `render UserBadge` — no `render Footer`.

Why the click reaches so far. `theme` lives in `AppProviders`, so `setTheme` re-renders that component. Both provider elements receive inline object literals, so on that render each `value` is a fresh object. Context compares values by `Object.is`, not field by field, so the `SessionContext` value also looks new even though `session` itself did not change. `Sidebar` is a legitimate consumer of `ThemeContext`, and `UserBadge` is a consumer of a value that changed identity, so both re-render. `memo` is irrelevant here: it memoizes props, while a context consumer must re-render to receive the new value; that is also why wrapping consumers in `memo` is the classic failed fix. `Footer` reads no context, and its element arrives through the stable `children` prop of a parent that did not re-render, so `memo` bails out. Note the two distinct events people conflate: the provider component re-rendering (cheap) and its consumers re-rendering (what the log shows).

Refactor. First colocate the state: give the theme its own `ThemeProvider` that owns `useState`, and keep `SessionProvider` separate, so a theme update never renders the component that holds the session. Second, stabilize what each provider hands down: `const signOut = useCallback(() => setSession(null), [])` and `const sessionValue = useMemo(() => ({ session, signOut }), [session, signOut])`; likewise for `toggle` and the theme value. With stable values, even a re-render of the provider for an unrelated reason leaves the other context value identical and its consumers untouched. Third, keep each provider as close as possible to the subtree that reads it. If consumers ever need narrower subscriptions than one value per context, that is the point to reach for an external store with selectors instead of splitting contexts indefinitely.
rubric: Predicts the first mount as all four components, and the post-click log as AppProviders, Sidebar and UserBadge with Footer absent
Explains that inline object literals get a new identity under Object.is, so the session value changes even though `session` did not
States that memo does not block context updates for consumers — it only covers the props path — which is why UserBadge re-renders
Refactors by colocating theme state in its own provider and/or memoizing each provided value and its callbacks with useMemo/useCallback
Separates provider re-render from consumer re-render, and names narrow subscriptions or provider placement as the durable fix, not more memo
